warmup.q: class ConfigurableFees(var policy: FeePolicy) : FeePolicy by policy. You build it with FlatFee(25), then set fees.policy = FlatFee(99). What does fees.feeMinor(10_000) return?
options: 99, because by policy forwards to the property
25, because the delegate was captured when the object was built
It doesn't compile: a var can't be a delegate
It throws, because the delegate changed under it
warmup.why: The compiler copies the constructor argument into a hidden private final FeePolicy $$delegate_0 field, and the generated feeMinor calls that field. Assigning policy changes the property only. It compiles without a warning, which is why the first option catches people.

sections.h: Class delegation forwards to the object you passed in, once
sections.html:
Lesson 5 of the patterns track showed what by writes for you: every method of the interface, forwarded to the object you named, except the ones you override. It also showed the trap: putAll goes straight to the inner map and never sees your put override. Two more details matter once you put by into real classes.

The first is that the delegate is captured once. class ConfigurableFees(var policy: FeePolicy) : FeePolicy by policy looks like it forwards to the policy property. javap shows two fields instead:

private final FeePolicy $$delegate_0;   // set from the constructor argument, never changed
private FeePolicy policy;               // the property you can reassign

The generated feeMinor calls $$delegate_0. Assign a new policy and the property changes, but every call still goes to the old object: the demo prints after swap, policy = FlatFee(99), fee: 25. A hand-written Java decorator reads its field on every call, so swapping works there:

Java
final class ConfigurableFeesJava implements FeePolicy {
    private FeePolicy policy;
    ConfigurableFeesJava(FeePolicy policy) { this.policy = policy; }
    void setPolicy(FeePolicy policy) { this.policy = policy; }

    @Override public long feeMinor(long amountMinor) {
        return policy.feeMinor(amountMinor);       // the current field, on every call
    }
}
Kotlin
class ConfigurableFees(var policy: FeePolicy) : FeePolicy by policy   // forwards to the FIRST policy

val fees = ConfigurableFees(FlatFee(25))
fees.policy = FlatFee(99)
fees.feeMinor(10_000)   // 25: $$delegate_0 still holds FlatFee(25)

If the target has to change at run time, write the forwarding yourself. Otherwise make the constructor parameter a plain parameter or a val, so nobody expects it to move.

The second detail: equals, hashCode and toString are not forwarded. They come from Any, not from the interface. A Tags class that delegates MutableSet<String> prints as Tags@2752f6e2, and two Tags with the same elements are not equal. That breaks the Set contract, which says two sets with the same elements are equal, and a HashSet<Tags> will happily keep both. Override the three and forward them to the inner set when the wrapper should behave like what it wraps.

With those two rules in mind, by is still the best tool for one job: wrapping a wide Java interface to change one or two methods. A DataSource that counts borrowed connections, a Kafka Producer that adds a trace header to every record: you write the methods you change, and the compiler writes the other twenty, with no chance of forgetting one when the interface grows a new method in the next library version.

Run ClassDelegationDemoJava, which swaps a hand-written Java decorator and then the Kotlin class from Java.
In Tags, add override fun equals(other: Any?) = other is Set<*> && inner == other and override fun hashCode() = inner.hashCode(). Run again.

code.title: ClassDelegationDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.kotlin.l03.demo interface FeePolicy { fun feeMinor(amountMinor: Long): Long } class FlatFee(private val fee: Long) : FeePolicy { override fun feeMinor(amountMinor: Long): Long = fee override fun toString(): String = "FlatFee($fee)" } /** `by policy` forwards to the object passed in at construction, stored in a hidden final field. */ class ConfigurableFees(var policy: FeePolicy) : FeePolicy by policy /** Delegating a Set forwards Set's methods, but not equals, hashCode or toString. */ class Tags(private val inner: MutableSet<String> = HashSet()) : MutableSet<String> by inner fun main() { val fees = ConfigurableFees(FlatFee(25)) println("fee: ${fees.feeMinor(10_000)}") fees.policy = FlatFee(99) // swap the policy... println("after swap, policy = ${fees.policy}, fee: ${fees.feeMinor(10_000)}") val a = Tags().apply { add("refund"); add("manual") } val b = Tags().apply { add("refund"); add("manual") } println("a = $a") println("a == b: ${a == b}, a.size = ${a.size}, \"refund\" in a: ${"refund" in a}") }

alt.html: package workbench.kotlin.l03.demo; /** * Java twin of ClassDelegationDemo.kt. Java has no `by`, so you write the forwarding yourself. * Written by hand, it reads the field on every call, so swapping the policy works. */ public class ClassDelegationDemoJava { static final class ConfigurableFeesJava implements FeePolicy { private FeePolicy policy; ConfigurableFeesJava(FeePolicy policy) { this.policy = policy; } void setPolicy(FeePolicy policy) { this.policy = policy; } @Override public long feeMinor(long amountMinor) { return policy.feeMinor(amountMinor); // reads the current field each time } } public static void main(String[] args) { ConfigurableFeesJava fees = new ConfigurableFeesJava(new FlatFee(25)); System.out.println("fee: " + fees.feeMinor(10_000)); fees.setPolicy(new FlatFee(99)); System.out.println("after swap, fee: " + fees.feeMinor(10_000)); // the Kotlin class, seen from Java: setPolicy changes the property, not the $$delegate_0 field ConfigurableFees kotlinFees = new ConfigurableFees(new FlatFee(25)); kotlinFees.setPolicy(new FlatFee(99)); System.out.println("Kotlin class after swap, fee: " + kotlinFees.feeMinor(10_000)); } }

try.expect: Kotlin prints fee: 25, then after swap, policy = FlatFee(99), fee: 25: the property moved, the calls didn't. javap lists private final ...FeePolicy $$delegate_0 and private ...FeePolicy policy. The Java decorator prints 99 after its swap, and the Kotlin class still prints 25 when Java swaps it. a == b is false until you add equals and hashCode, then true.

sections.h: A delegated property is a hidden field and two calls
sections.html:
Property delegation shares the keyword and almost nothing else. Start without it. Say every change to an order's status must be logged, and you want the logging written once, in a small helper class you can reuse for any audited property. By hand, the property forwards its getter and setter to the helper:

Java
final class OrderJava {
    private final Box<String> status = new Box<>("NEW");     // the helper holds the value
    String getStatus() { return status.get(); }
    void setStatus(String s) { status.set("status", s); }    // and logs every change
}
Kotlin
class Order {
    private val statusBox = Audited("NEW")                   // the helper holds the value
    var status: String
        get() = statusBox.getValue(this, ::status)
        set(value) = statusBox.setValue(this, ::status, value)   // and logs every change
}

::status is a reference to the property itself, a KProperty, which knows its name, so the helper can log status without a string literal that could drift. That forwarding is all by does. The helper object is called the delegate. It needs only two functions with fixed names, getValue and setValue, and then by writes the getter and setter for you:

Java
// Java has no `by`: the helper is an ordinary class, and you write the forwarding above yourself
final class Box<T> {
    private T value;
    Box(T value) { this.value = value; }
    T get() { return value; }
    void set(String name, T value) {
        System.out.println("  " + name + ": " + this.value + " -> " + value);
        this.value = value;
    }
}
Kotlin
class Audited<T>(private var value: T) : ReadWriteProperty<Any?, T> {
    override fun getValue(thisRef: Any?, property: KProperty<*>): T = value

    override fun setValue(thisRef: Any?, property: KProperty<*>, value: T) {
        println("  ${property.name}: ${this.value} -> $value")
        this.value = value
    }
}

class Order {
    var status: String by Audited("NEW")      // the same forwarding, written by the compiler
}

getValue receives the owning object (thisRef) and a KProperty that describes the property, including its name. A val needs only getValue. You can write them as operator fun members or extensions on any class, or implement ReadOnlyProperty or ReadWriteProperty as here.

The compiler's version matches your hand-written one with one change, shown in the figure. For each delegated property it adds a hidden field, status$delegate, typed as whatever the expression after by returns. Instead of a fresh ::status on every call, it builds one static array per class, $$delegatedProperties, with a KProperty object per property, filled once in the static initializer. Then getStatus() loads status$delegate, loads $$delegatedProperties[0], calls getValue, and casts the result to String.

Java sees none of this. It sees getStatus() and setStatus(String), ordinary methods; the delegate field is private and the array is package-private. That suits frameworks that work through getters and setters. It's also a warning: a setter that logs, validates or audits looks exactly like a plain setter from the outside.

A few kinds of delegate get no $delegate field: delegating to another property (by this::amountMinor), to a named object, to this, or to a constant. The docs list the cases. Everything else costs one extra object per delegated property, per instance.

The operators don't have to live in the delegate's class. They can be extension functions, and that's how by settings works on a plain Map in the last section: the standard library declares getValue as an inline extension operator on Map, which looks up the key property.name. You can do the same for a type you don't own. An operator fun Headers.getValue(thisRef: Any?, property: KProperty<*>): String would let a class write val traceId: String by kafkaHeaders.

code.title: PropertyDelegateDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.kotlin.l03.demo import kotlin.properties.ReadWriteProperty import kotlin.reflect.KProperty /** A hand-written delegate: getValue and setValue are all the compiler needs. */ class Audited<T>(private var value: T) : ReadWriteProperty<Any?, T> { override fun getValue(thisRef: Any?, property: KProperty<*>): T = value override fun setValue(thisRef: Any?, property: KProperty<*>, value: T) { println(" ${property.name}: ${this.value} -> $value") this.value = value } } class Order { var status: String by Audited("NEW") var amountMinor: Long by Audited(0L) } fun main() { val order = Order() order.status = "AUTHORIZED" order.amountMinor = 4_250 println("status = ${order.status}, amountMinor = ${order.amountMinor}") println("fields the compiler generated:") Order::class.java.declaredFields.forEach { println(" ${it.type.simpleName} ${it.name}") } }

alt.title: PropertyDelegateDemoJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.kotlin.l03.demo; import java.lang.reflect.Field; /** * Java twin of PropertyDelegateDemo.kt. Java sees getStatus and setStatus, ordinary methods, * and can't tell that a delegate sits behind them. */ public class PropertyDelegateDemoJava { // the hand-written Java shape: a field holding a helper object, and accessors that call it static final class Box<T> { private T value; Box(T value) { this.value = value; } T get() { return value; } void set(String name, T value) { System.out.println(" " + name + ": " + this.value + " -> " + value); this.value = value; } } static final class OrderJava { private final Box<String> status = new Box<>("NEW"); String getStatus() { return status.get(); } void setStatus(String s) { status.set("status", s); } } public static void main(String[] args) { Order order = new Order(); // the Kotlin class order.setStatus("AUTHORIZED"); // goes through status$delegate.setValue order.setAmountMinor(4_250L); System.out.println("status = " + order.getStatus() + ", amountMinor = " + order.getAmountMinor()); OrderJava hand = new OrderJava(); hand.setStatus("AUTHORIZED"); System.out.println("fields of the Kotlin Order, seen by reflection:"); for (Field f : Order.class.getDeclaredFields()) { System.out.println(" " + f.getType().getSimpleName() + " " + f.getName()); } } }

Adding note adds a note$delegate field and a third array entry, not a second array.

sections.h: What by lazy costs: an object per instance and a call per read
sections.html:
by lazy is the delegate you use most, and the memory model track already took it apart: it is double-checked locking, SYNCHRONIZED by default, with PUBLICATION and NONE as the other modes (lesson 5 of that track). This section is about the bill.

Java
// Java's per-instance lazy field: volatile double-checked locking, by hand
private volatile Double eurUsd;

double eurUsd() {
    Double v = eurUsd;
    if (v == null) {
        synchronized (this) {
            v = eurUsd;
            if (v == null) eurUsd = v = rates.fetch("EURUSD");
        }
    }
    return v;
}
Kotlin
class FxQuote(private val rates: RateService) {
    val eurUsd: Double by lazy { rates.fetch("EURUSD") }    // SYNCHRONIZED
}

Each FxQuote gets a private final kotlin.Lazy eurUsd$delegate field. The constructor fills it with a new SynchronizedLazyImpl (fields initializer, _value and lock), and the initializer lambda is a second object. Every read calls Lazy.getValue() through an interface, and for a Double it then unboxes with checkcast Number and doubleValue. There's no $$delegatedProperties array, because lazy never looks at the property.

For one configuration object, none of that matters. For a class you create per payment, per Kafka record or per database row, it's two extra objects every time, for a value you may never read. Use lazy on long-lived objects: singletons, @ApplicationScoped beans, caches. For short-lived ones, compute the value in the constructor or make it a function.

When only one thread can ever touch the object, lazy(LazyThreadSafetyMode.NONE) drops the lock and the class becomes UnsafeLazyImpl. The docs say it "doesn't incur any thread-safety guarantees and related overhead". Think of a parser or a report builder that lives inside one function call. Don't use it on anything a CDI container shares: an @ApplicationScoped bean is read from many request threads at once, and NONE gives you no guarantee that they all see one value.

One behavior is easy to miss. lazy doesn't cache an exception. In the demo the first read throws rate service timed out, and the second read runs the initializer again and succeeds. For a remote call that's usually what you want.

try.title: Count the initializer runs
steps: Run LazyDemo. Before you do, predict how many times the initializer runs over three reads when the first one throws.
Run LazyDemoJava, which does the same with hand-written double-checked locking and then reads the Kotlin class from Java.

code.title: LazyDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.kotlin.l03.demo var rateCalls = 0 class FxQuote { /** Default mode: SYNCHRONIZED. The first reader runs the initializer under a lock. */ val eurUsd: Double by lazy { rateCalls++ if (rateCalls == 1) throw IllegalStateException("rate service timed out") 1.0842 } } fun main() { for (mode in LazyThreadSafetyMode.entries) { println("$mode -> ${lazy(mode) { 0 }.javaClass.name}") } val quote = FxQuote() try { quote.eurUsd } catch (e: IllegalStateException) { println("first read failed: ${e.message}") } println("second read: ${quote.eurUsd} (initializer ran $rateCalls times)") println("third read: ${quote.eurUsd} (initializer ran $rateCalls times)") println("field: ${FxQuote::class.java.declaredFields.joinToString { "${it.type.name} ${it.name}" }}") }

alt.title: LazyDemoJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.kotlin.l03.demo; /** * Java twin of LazyDemo.kt. Java has no lazy delegate. For a per-instance lazy field the usual * shape is double-checked locking on a volatile field, which is what Kotlin's SYNCHRONIZED mode does. */ public class LazyDemoJava { static int rateCalls = 0; static final class FxQuoteJava { private volatile Double eurUsd; // null means "not computed yet" double eurUsd() { Double v = eurUsd; if (v == null) { synchronized (this) { v = eurUsd; if (v == null) { rateCalls++; if (rateCalls == 1) throw new IllegalStateException("rate service timed out"); eurUsd = v = 1.0842; } } } return v; } } public static void main(String[] args) { FxQuoteJava quote = new FxQuoteJava(); try { quote.eurUsd(); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.println("first read failed: " + e.getMessage()); } System.out.println("second read: " + quote.eurUsd() + " (initializer ran " + rateCalls + " times)"); System.out.println("third read: " + quote.eurUsd() + " (initializer ran " + rateCalls + " times)"); // the Kotlin class from Java: getEurUsd() calls Lazy.getValue() on every read FxQuote kotlinQuote = new FxQuote(); try { kotlinQuote.getEurUsd(); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.println("Kotlin FxQuote from Java, first read failed: " + e.getMessage()); } System.out.println("Kotlin FxQuote from Java, second read: " + kotlinQuote.getEurUsd()); } }

try.expect: The three modes map to kotlin.SynchronizedLazyImpl, kotlin.SafePublicationLazyImpl and kotlin.UnsafeLazyImpl. The first read fails, the second succeeds, and the initializer ran 2 times, not 3: once the value is stored, reads stop calling it. The only field is kotlin.Lazy eurUsd$delegate, and getEurUsd is getfield, invokeinterface Lazy.getValue, checkcast Number, doubleValue. The Java version behaves the same.

sections.h: The standard delegates, and provideDelegate for early checks
sections.html:
The standard library ships the delegates you'd otherwise write by hand. Delegates.observable(initial) { property, old, new -> } calls you after every assignment. Delegates.vetoable(initial) { property, old, new -> Boolean } calls you before it, and returning false keeps the old value. And a val can read from a Map: val host: String by settings looks up the key "host". A var does the same with a MutableMap. Delegates.notNull<Int>() covers what lateinit can't, a primitive: reading it before the first assignment throws Property size should be initialized before get.

Java
void setOwner(String owner) {                          // observable, by hand
    String old = this.owner;
    this.owner = owner;
    System.out.println("owner: " + old + " -> " + owner);
}

void setLimit(int limit) {                             // vetoable, by hand
    if (limit <= 100) this.limit = limit;
}

int port() { return (Integer) settings.get("port"); }  // map-backed, by hand
Kotlin
var owner: String by Delegates.observable("<none>") { property, old, new ->
    println("${property.name}: $old -> $new")
}
var limit: Int by Delegates.vetoable(100) { _, _, new -> new <= 100 }

val port: Int by settings                              // settings["port"], cast to Int

The demo prints owner: <none> -> alice, owner: alice -> bob, limit after veto: 100 and limit after ok: 50. A map-backed property fails only when you read it: a missing key throws java.util.NoSuchElementException: Key port is missing in the map. That's late. For configuration you'd rather fail when the object is built, and that's what provideDelegate is for.

If the object after by has an operator fun provideDelegate(thisRef, property), the compiler calls it once per property, while the owning object is being constructed, and keeps what it returns as the real delegate. The docs describe it as the way to get "the necessary validation right away". PropertyDelegateProvider { thisRef, property -> ... } creates one without a new class. In the demo, binding issuerUrl prints during Settings(), before anyone reads the property. The lab uses the same trick to register every audited property up front.

try.title: Watch the standard delegates fire
steps: Run StdDelegatesDemo (or its Java twin). Predict the order of building Settings..., binding issuerUrl and built; ... before you look.
Change the veto to new <= 40 and run. Predict both limit lines first.
Remove "host" to "issuer.example" from the map. Predict which line fails, and when.

code.title: StdDelegatesDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.kotlin.l03.demo import kotlin.properties.Delegates import kotlin.properties.PropertyDelegateProvider import kotlin.properties.ReadOnlyProperty class Payout { // observable: the handler runs after the assignment var owner: String by Delegates.observable("<none>") { property, old, new -> println("${property.name}: $old -> $new") } // vetoable: the handler runs before the assignment; false keeps the old value var limit: Int by Delegates.vetoable(100) { _, _, new -> new <= 100 } } class IssuerConfig(settings: Map<String, Any?>) { val host: String by settings // reads settings["host"] val port: Int by settings // reads settings["port"] } /** provideDelegate runs once per property, while the object is built: validation happens right away. */ fun requiredEnv(): PropertyDelegateProvider<Any?, ReadOnlyProperty<Any?, String>> = PropertyDelegateProvider { _, property -> println("binding ${property.name}") ReadOnlyProperty { _, _ -> "value of ${property.name}" } } class Settings { val issuerUrl: String by requiredEnv() } fun main() { val p = Payout() p.owner = "alice" p.owner = "bob" p.limit = 500 println("limit after veto: ${p.limit}") p.limit = 50 println("limit after ok: ${p.limit}") val config = IssuerConfig(mapOf("host" to "issuer.example")) println("host = ${config.host}") try { println("port = ${config.port}") } catch (e: NoSuchElementException) { println("port failed on access: ${e.message}") } println("building Settings...") val s = Settings() println("built; issuerUrl = ${s.issuerUrl}") }

alt.title: StdDelegatesDemoJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.kotlin.l03.demo; import java.util.Map; import java.util.NoSuchElementException; /** * Java twin of StdDelegatesDemo.kt. Java writes each behavior into the setter or getter by hand. */ public class StdDelegatesDemoJava { static final class PayoutJava { private String owner = "<none>"; private int limit = 100; void setOwner(String owner) { String old = this.owner; this.owner = owner; // observable: assign, then notify System.out.println("owner: " + old + " -> " + owner); } void setLimit(int limit) { if (limit <= 100) this.limit = limit; // vetoable: check, then assign } int getLimit() { return limit; } } static final class IssuerConfigJava { private final Map<String, Object> settings; IssuerConfigJava(Map<String, Object> settings) { this.settings = settings; } String host() { return (String) get("host"); } int port() { return (Integer) get("port"); } private Object get(String key) { if (!settings.containsKey(key)) throw new NoSuchElementException("Key " + key + " is missing in the map."); return settings.get(key); } } // provideDelegate has no Java twin: Java validates in the constructor, which also runs at build time static final class SettingsJava { final String issuerUrl; SettingsJava() { System.out.println("binding issuerUrl"); issuerUrl = "value of issuerUrl"; } } public static void main(String[] args) { PayoutJava p = new PayoutJava(); p.setOwner("alice"); p.setOwner("bob"); p.setLimit(500); System.out.println("limit after veto: " + p.getLimit()); p.setLimit(50); System.out.println("limit after ok: " + p.getLimit()); IssuerConfigJava config = new IssuerConfigJava(Map.of("host", "issuer.example")); System.out.println("host = " + config.host()); try { System.out.println("port = " + config.port()); } catch (NoSuchElementException e) { System.out.println("port failed on access: " + e.getMessage()); } System.out.println("building Settings..."); SettingsJava s = new SettingsJava(); System.out.println("built; issuerUrl = " + s.issuerUrl); } }

try.expect: building Settings... comes first, then binding issuerUrl while the constructor runs, then built; issuerUrl = value of issuerUrl. With new <= 40 both assignments are vetoed, so both lines print 100: the handler checks assignments, never the initial value. Without host, building IssuerConfig still works and the program fails on the config.host read with Key host is missing in the map.

analogy: A delegated property is a flat with a building manager. You own the flat, but every request to get in or change something goes through the manager, who can keep a log, refuse a change, or fetch the keys only on the first visit. Visitors from outside (Java callers) see an ordinary front door, a getter and a setter. The analogy breaks at class delegation: there the manager is fixed on the day the building opens, and changing the name on the mailbox (the var) doesn't change who answers.
world: Audit trails are the obvious fit in payments: a PaymentDraft whose status and amountMinor record every change for the compliance log, written once as a delegate instead of in every setter. Quarkus configuration usually arrives through @ConfigMapping interfaces, but code that reads a parsed Map (a merchant's routing rules from a JSON column, Kafka headers) can use map-backed properties, with provideDelegate to check the required keys when the object is built rather than on the first payment that needs them. And be careful with by on CDI beans: a bean that delegates an interface to a constructor argument keeps that argument forever. That's fine for an injected client, and wrong for anything you meant to swap at run time, such as a fee policy behind a feature flag.
mistake:
Swapping the target of class delegation at run time. class Router(var gateway: Gateway) : Gateway by gateway invites a feature flag to set router.gateway = newGateway:

Java
// the Java decorator people have in mind: it reads the field on every call
@Override public String authorize(Payment p) { return gateway.authorize(p); }
Kotlin
class Router(var gateway: Gateway) : Gateway by gateway

router.gateway = newGateway     // the property changes; authorize() still calls the old gateway

The assignment works, the property changes, and every call still goes to the gateway passed to the constructor, because the compiler copied it into a hidden final $$delegate_0 field. Nothing fails; the traffic simply never moves. If the target must change, write the forwarding methods yourself so they read the property each time, or forward to an AtomicReference<Gateway>.

compare.title: An audited field: Java setters vs a Kotlin delegate

java.title: PaymentDraft.java
java.html: public final class PaymentDraft { private final ChangeLog log; private String status = "NEW"; private long amountMinor = 0; public PaymentDraft(ChangeLog log) { this.log = log; } public String getStatus() { return status; } public void setStatus(String s) { if (!s.equals(status)) log.record("status", status, s); // repeated in every setter status = s; } public long getAmountMinor() { return amountMinor; } public void setAmountMinor(long a) { if (a != amountMinor) log.record("amountMinor", amountMinor, a); amountMinor = a; } }

kotlin.title: PaymentDraft.kt
kotlin.html: class Recorded<T>(private var value: T, private val log: ChangeLog) : ReadWriteProperty<Any?, T> { override fun getValue(thisRef: Any?, property: KProperty<*>): T = value override fun setValue(thisRef: Any?, property: KProperty<*>, value: T) { if (value != this.value) log.changes += Change(property.name, this.value, value) this.value = value } } class PaymentDraft(val log: ChangeLog) { var status: String by Recorded("NEW", log) // the audit is written once, in Recorded var amountMinor: Long by Recorded(0L, log) }

compare.note: In Java the audit lives in every setter, and a new field without it is a silent gap that only review can catch. In Kotlin it's written once, in the delegate, and each property opts in with by. The property name comes from the KProperty the compiler passes in, so it can't drift from the field name the way a string literal can. The run-time price is one delegate object per property per instance, plus one static KProperty array per class. Java code calling the Kotlin class can't tell the two apart: it sees getStatus and setStatus either way.

worked.title: A config object that fails at startup, not on the first payment

steps.say: Start with a map-backed config. It reads nicely, but a missing key is found only when someone reads the property, which may be the first payment routed to that acquirer at 2 a.m.
steps.code: final class RoutingConfig { private final Map<String, Object> settings; RoutingConfig(Map<String, Object> settings) { this.settings = settings; } String acquirer() { return (String) settings.get("acquirer"); } // null if missing long timeoutMs() { return (Long) settings.get("timeoutMs"); } // NullPointerException if missing }

alt.html: class RoutingConfig(settings: Map<String, Any?>) { val acquirer: String by settings // NoSuchElementException, but only when read val timeoutMs: Long by settings }

steps.say: Write a provider. provideDelegate runs once per property while the object is built, so it can check the key right away and hand back a delegate that only returns the value it read.
steps.code: fun <T> Map<String, Any?>.required(): PropertyDelegateProvider<Any?, ReadOnlyProperty<Any?, T>> = PropertyDelegateProvider { _, property -> // 1. check the key while the owning object is constructed require(property.name in this) { "missing config key '${property.name}'" } @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST") val value = this[property.name] as T // 2. the real delegate just returns what was read ReadOnlyProperty { _, _ -> value } } class RoutingConfig(settings: Map<String, Any?>) { val acquirer: String by settings.required() val timeoutMs: Long by settings.required() }

alt.html: // Java does the same check in the constructor, one line per key RoutingConfig(Map<String, Object> settings) { this.acquirer = (String) require(settings, "acquirer"); this.timeoutMs = (Long) require(settings, "timeoutMs"); } private static Object require(Map<String, Object> m, String key) { if (!m.containsKey(key)) throw new IllegalArgumentException("missing config key '" + key + "'"); return m.get(key); }

steps.say: Build one with a key missing. It fails in the constructor, with the property's name in the message, because the name came from the KProperty the compiler passed in.
steps.code: RoutingConfig(mapOf("acquirer" to "acq-a", "timeoutMs" to 2_000L)) // fine RoutingConfig(mapOf("acquirer" to "acq-a")) // java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: missing config key 'timeoutMs'

alt.html: new RoutingConfig(Map.of("acquirer", "acq-a", "timeoutMs", 2_000L)); // fine new RoutingConfig(Map.of("acquirer", "acq-a")); // java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: missing config key 'timeoutMs'

steps.say: The cast is still unchecked: a "timeoutMs" to "2000" entry passes the check and fails later with a ClassCastException on the first read. If that matters, pass the expected class into required and check it with isInstance, the class-token trick from the generics track.

lab.title: An audited property delegate
steps: Run the tests. All six fail, most with NotImplementedError thrown while a PaymentDraft is being built. That's provideDelegate at work already.
In Recorded.kt, write getValue and setValue (TODOs 1 and 2). Record a Change only when the value really changes.
Write ChangeLog.recorded (TODO 3): return a PropertyDelegateProvider that checks and registers property.name, then creates the Recorded.
In PaymentDraft.kt, make currency a vetoable delegate (TODO 4), and delegate both MerchantConfig properties to the map (TODO 5).

Run the tests until all six pass, including DraftFromJavaTest, which only sees setStatus and getLog. Then run javap -p -cp kotlin/build/classes/kotlin/main workbench.kotlin.l03.PaymentDraft and match each field to a property.
hints: In setValue, the parameter value shadows the field. Compare with if (value != this.value), record Change(property.name, this.value, value), then assign this.value = value.
PropertyDelegateProvider { _, property -> check(property.name !in tracked) { "..." }; tracked += property.name; Recorded(initial, this) }. Inside the lambda, this is still the ChangeLog receiver.
var currency: String by Delegates.vetoable("EUR") { _, _, new -> new.matches(Regex("[A-Z]{3}")) }, with import kotlin.properties.Delegates.
val name: String by settings needs no import. Delete the get() = TODO(...) and write by settings in its place.
lab.done: All six tests in DelegationTest and DraftFromJavaTest pass.

drill.title: Write a clamping delegate from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write class Clamped(min: Int, max: Int, initial: Int) as a ReadWriteProperty<Any?, Int> that keeps every assigned value inside min..max, and use it as var discountBps: Int by Clamped(0, 10_000, initial = 0). Then write the Java setter that does the same. What does discountBps = 12_000 leave behind?

answer.html: class Clamped(private val min: Int, private val max: Int, initial: Int) : ReadWriteProperty<Any?, Int> { private var value = initial.coerceIn(min, max) override fun getValue(thisRef: Any?, property: KProperty<*>): Int = value override fun setValue(thisRef: Any?, property: KProperty<*>, value: Int) { this.value = value.coerceIn(min, max) } } class Discount { var discountBps: Int by Clamped(0, 10_000, initial = 0) // 12_000 is stored as 10_000 }

alt.title: Discount.java
alt.html: final class Discount { private int discountBps = 0; int getDiscountBps() { return discountBps; } void setDiscountBps(int bps) { discountBps = Math.max(0, Math.min(10_000, bps)); // 12_000 is stored as 10_000 } }

recap: Class delegation (: Iface by x) forwards every interface method you don't override to x, captured once into a hidden final $$delegate_0 field. Reassigning a var doesn't move it.
equals, hashCode and toString are not forwarded, and the delegate never calls back into your overrides.
A delegated property compiles to a prop$delegate field, a static $$delegatedProperties array of KProperty objects, and accessors that call getValue and setValue. Java sees plain getters and setters.
by lazy costs a Lazy object and an initializer lambda per instance, plus an interface call on every read. It doesn't cache exceptions. Use NONE for single-threaded objects.
observable runs after an assignment, vetoable before it, and by map reads a key named after the property when you read it.
provideDelegate runs once per property while the object is built: the place for early validation and registration.

explain.prompt: A teammate asks what the compiler actually generates for var status: String by log.recorded("NEW") in a class, and what a Java caller sees when it calls setStatus. Explain it in your own words.
explain.answer: log.recorded("NEW") returns a delegate provider, so while the object is being constructed the compiler calls its provideDelegate with the property's KProperty, and stores the Recorded it returns in a hidden private field called status$delegate. The class also gets one static array, $$delegatedProperties, holding a KProperty for each delegated property. The getter getStatus() loads the delegate and the matching KProperty and calls getValue, then casts the result to String. The setter calls setValue(this, property, value), which is where Recorded compares the old and new value and writes a change to the log. A Java caller sees nothing special: just a public setStatus(String) method. It can't tell there's a delegate behind it, but the audit still happens, because the logic lives in the setter the compiler generated.

deeper.html:
Delegating to another property is the one case worth knowing that has no $delegate field at all. It is useful when you rename a property and need the old name for a while:

Java
// Java keeps the old accessor by hand and marks it deprecated
public long getAmountMinor() { return amountMinor; }
@Deprecated public long getAmount() { return amountMinor; }
Kotlin
class Payment {
    var amountMinor: Long = 0

    @Deprecated("Use amountMinor", ReplaceWith("amountMinor"))
    var amount: Long by this::amountMinor
}

javap -p on that class shows getAmount and setAmount, a static helper getAmount$delegate(Payment), and no amount$delegate field: the compiler reads and writes amountMinor directly. The IDE offers the ReplaceWith fix at every call site, so the rename can finish over a few releases.

The other cases without a field, from the docs: a delegate that is a named object, this, a constant expression or an enum entry, and "a final val property with a backing field and a default getter in the same module". Everything else pays for one delegate object per property per instance.

One more design note on class delegation. It composes well with the patterns track's decorators because the delegate never calls back into your class. With inheritance, HashSet.addAll calls add, so an override of add sees every element. With by, addAll goes to the inner set, and your add override is skipped. Neither is wrong, but only the by version is stable across JDK updates, because it doesn't depend on how the parent class happens to be written.
